sections.html:
Marlboro Township is a high-income Monmouth County suburb where owners occupy 93.1 percent of homes, so nearly every sale starts with a homeowner rather than a landlord. Median home value is $701,200, median household income is $186,292 and median gross rent is $2,699. Population was about 42,254 in mid-2025.

Retirement communities are part of the mix. Greenbriar North has more than 750 homes, and Marlboro Greens has 341 homes built from 1986 to 1988. The township is spread out as scattered villages rather than one downtown, with Morganville and Robertsville the two largest named areas, so buyers compare streets and neighborhoods more than a town center. Many owners are long-term residents, which means older houses with original systems are common and the inspection items below deserve attention early.

Marlboro Township requires a Continued Certificate of Occupancy for every home sale or rental. The Zoning/Code Enforcement Division issues it, and the paperwork is available on the township website or at the zoning office. Reach the zoning officer at 732-536-0200, extension 1809, on weekdays between 8:30 and 4:30.

Before booking the inspection, ask the zoning office whether permits for sheds, fences, patios and decks are closed. A shed under 200 square feet needs a zoning permit with a scaled survey, and larger or wired sheds also need construction permits. Day to day, the division works from complaints, so a missing permit tends to come up when someone asks.

sections.h2: Old oil tanks and environmental records
sections.html:
Buyers and their lenders sometimes ask about contaminated sites, and Marlboro has some history here. The state environmental department lists 39 known locations in town with underground storage tank contamination. The Burnt Fly Bog Superfund cleanup site covers about 1,700 acres off Tyler Lane and Spring Valley Road on the Old Bridge border, where waste oil was stored in lagoons in the 1950s and early 1960s.

The practical step for an owner is to know what is buried or stored on the lot. Find out whether an old heating oil tank was removed or left in place, and keep any closure paperwork where a buyer can see it. For a house near the Spring Valley Road area, ask the zoning office for the block and lot file and the state environmental department for site records before a buyer's attorney asks.

The seller pays New Jersey's realty transfer fee at recording. Prices above $1,000,000 add a graduated percent fee, starting at 1 percent of the whole price, and the law has charged it to the seller since July 10, 2025.

Deeds are recorded by the Monmouth County Clerk, whose record room is at the Market Yard, 33 Mechanic Street in Freehold, open weekdays until 4:00 in the afternoon. The fee is $40 for the first page of a deed and $10 for each additional page. The seller's residency form (GIT/REP) is filed with the deed, and a signer who lives out of state may owe estimated income tax on the gain, which the form is designed to determine.

sections.h2: Getting around: roads, buses and rail
sections.html: Marlboro is a driving town. U.S. Route 9, Route 18, Route 79 and County Road 520 are the main thoroughfares, with Route 34 in the northeast corner. The township has 229.71 miles of road, most of it township-maintained. NJ Transit buses 131, 135 and 139 run to the Port Authority Bus Terminal in Manhattan, and the nearest commuter rail stop is Aberdeen-Matawan on the North Jersey Coast Line. Workers average 41.2 minutes to get to their jobs, a figure many buyers weigh when they compare Marlboro with towns closer to the shore or the city.

sections.h2: Ways to sell a Marlboro house fast
sections.html:
Marlboro owners choose among a listing agent, a do-it-yourself sale and a cash buyer who accepts the house with its flaws. All three require the Continued Certificate of Occupancy, so the real differences are speed, cost and how much repair work the owner takes on.

  • An agent listing exposes the house to the most buyers and works well for a move-in ready property, although commissions and requested repairs reduce what the owner nets.
  • A sale without an agent keeps the commission while shifting pricing, showings and negotiation to the owner.
  • A cash purchase can fit an inherited house, a vacant property, or a house with an old oil tank or unpermitted work that would complicate a mortgage-financed buyer.

Put in writing who orders the HVAC form, the chimney inspection and the well or septic certification, and who pays for any fix the inspector requires.

Start with the zoning office. Call the number above, ask for the current application, and find out which permits on your house are still open. Open permits are the item most likely to hold up a closing, so clear them before you list.

Next, line up the contractors. Book the HVAC company and the chimney sweep if you have a fireplace, and arrange Board of Health certification if the house has a well or septic system. Then pay the fees and schedule the inspection. Because the certificate is good for 90 days, time the visit so it will still be valid on the closing date. If the inspector finds something, each re-inspection costs $75.

Keep a folder with the certificate, the HVAC form, the chimney report, any septic or well certification and the permit closeouts. Hand a copy to the buyer's attorney early, because a missing page is a common reason a closing date slips by a week or more. If the house is vacant or inherited, say so when you call the zoning office, since the person who signs the application must be able to give access for the inspection.

At closing, the title company or attorney handles the transfer fee, the residency form and the deed for recording with the county clerk. A cash sale skips the lender's appraisal and mortgage underwriting, which removes the most common source of delay, though the township certificate is still required.

faqs.q: Does Marlboro require an inspection when I sell my house?
faqs.a: Yes. Marlboro Township requires a Continued Certificate of Occupancy for every home sale or rental, issued after an inspection. It is good for 90 days, and each re-inspection costs $75.

faqs.q: What paperwork do I need from outside contractors for a Marlboro sale?
faqs.a: An HVAC company fills out the heating and cooling form, a certified chimney sweep inspects any fireplace, and a house on a well or septic system needs certification from the Monmouth County Board of Health.

faqs.q: Who pays the realty transfer fee on a Marlboro home?
faqs.a: The seller pays it at recording, and it rises with price. Sales above $1,000,000 also pay a graduated percent fee that starts at 1 percent.

faqs.q: Where is a Marlboro deed recorded?
faqs.a: The Monmouth County Clerk records it, at the Market Yard, 33 Mechanic Street, Freehold. The fee is $40 for the first page of a deed and $10 per added page.

faqs.q: Should I worry about an old oil tank on my Marlboro property?
faqs.a: Yes, check it before listing. The state lists 39 underground storage tank contamination locations in Marlboro, so a buyer's attorney is likely to ask whether a tank was removed and whether closure records exist.
